newsitem.title: USA: Struggle against flooding Ohio River goes on.
newsitem.headline: Struggle against flooding Ohio River goes on.

text.p: National Guard troops bulldozed layers of mud and debris left by deadly floodwaters on Thursday while the riverfront city of Louisville braced for the Ohio River's highest crest in three decades.

Louisville's towering flood walls will be tested on Friday evening with an anticipated crest more than 15 feet (5 metres) above flood stage, the river's highest level since a catastrophic 1964 flood, the National Weather Service said.

Meanwhile the National Guard told anxious residents of Falmouth, Kentucky, 60 miles (100 km) northwest of Louisville, to wait while troops used backhoes to scrape away mounds of debris and trucked off ruined appliances and refrigerators. A weekend deluge submerged the town of 2,300 under the Licking River, a tributary of the Ohio that has since receded, leaving four dead.

Officials lowered the stricken town's death toll from five after mistakenly counting one victim twice. Rescuers completed a grim house-to-house search on Thursday, then issued a statewide plea for residents still listed as missing to report their whereabouts if they had fled elsewhere.

Kentucky's death toll was at 16 after a previously counted road fatality was declared a murder victim. Weekend storms with tornadoes and floods that hit from Arkansas to West Virginia were blamed for 55 deaths.

Elsewhere, violent thunderstorms killed two motorists in North Carolina overnight and four New York City schoolchildren were crushed to death when high winds sent a huge maple tree crashing into a van taking them to school.

Hundreds of people were forced to evacuate flooded homes ahead of the cresting Ohio River and its tributaries across Kentucky, Ohio and Indiana. Under sunny skies in Cincinnati, the river actually dropped slightly on Thursday from its crest of 64.7 feet (19.7 metres) late on Wednesday, which was 12 feet (3.7 metres) above flood stage.

Kentucky, with more miles of river than any other U.S. state except Alaska, added 15 counties to the nine already declared disaster areas. Nearly 900 Kentuckians were in shelters, many after fleeing homes along backed-up creeks and rivers that flow into the Ohio River.
Along the river in Indiana, about 400 people were forced out of their homes and even higher river levels were expected in the coming days as the crest flows downstream.
"The river's going up but nothing really dramatic. Just a slow, methodical rise in the water," Indiana Emergency Management Agency spokesman Alden Taylor said.
National Guard troops and jail inmates joined townspeople in Tell City, Indiana, to reinforce the town's flood barrier.

The Army Corps of Engineers manipulated its system of dams and reservoirs from Ohio to Tennessee to reduce the flow of Ohio River tributaries, lowering the expected crest at Louisville by six feet (two metres), corps spokesman Todd Hornback said.

The flood even caused cancellation of the Ringling Brothers Barnum and Bailey circus during the five days it was scheduled at Cincinnati's Riverfront Coliseum. But in a public relations stroke, circus managers sent in the clowns to perform for flood victims housed in overnight emergency shelters around the city.
